raw_response:
For a Go/Gin application receiving multipart image uploads, I would start with Go's image decoders plus disintegration/imaging. The useful distinction is between identifying a likely format, checking whether that format actually decodes, and producing a smaller output. A MIME detector handles the first task; a decoder and an image-processing library cover the others. Gin and htmx do not change those processing requirements.

## Ranked candidates

1. **Go image.DecodeConfig and image.Decode** — https://pkg.go.dev/image  
   Use the registered image decoders to identify the encoded format, inspect dimensions, and reject inputs that fail actual decoding. DecodeConfig is useful before allocating the full decoded image; then rewind or reopen the input and call Decode. Header success alone is insufficient. Register the codecs that your application intends to accept and enforce a format allowlist and dimension/pixel limits. The opened package documentation is go1.27.4, dated November 10, 2026, so this particular evidence is after the July 1 cutoff; older documentation retrieval attempts failed.

2. **disintegration/imaging** — https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/disintegration/imaging  
   Decode accepted uploads, reduce them with Fit or Resize, and encode a fresh output image using a straightforward Go processing API. Fit is convenient for a maximum display-size box, while Fill supports fixed-size cropped thumbnails. Its documented encoder supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF and BMP. Apply input limits before processing, and check that your required formats fit this set. The inspected v1.6.2 documentation is dated November 16, 2019.

3. **Go net/http DetectContentType and MaxBytesReader** — https://pkg.go.dev/net/http@go1.24.0#DetectContentType  
   Combine a bounded request body with content-based MIME sniffing to replace filename-extension checks at the upload boundary. DetectContentType examines at most 512 bytes, making it useful for an early allowlist decision, while MaxBytesReader limits incoming request-body reads. A convincing header can still precede broken image data, so decoding remains necessary. The opened go1.24.0 reference is dated February 11, 2025.

4. **h2non/bimg** — https://github.com/h2non/bimg  
   Use its libvips-backed image operations to resize and convert accepted uploads when transformation cost is a bottleneck. It provides resizing, cropping, rotation and format conversion, with JPEG, PNG and WebP output described in the README. Its deployment cost includes libvips, a C compiler and any required codec dependencies. Benchmark representative inputs before choosing it for performance; I have not tested the repository's performance claims. The inspected README is live and its publication date is unestablished.

5. **gabriel-vasile/mimetype** — https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/gabriel-vasile/mimetype  
   Detect MIME types directly from a multipart reader or byte buffer when a dedicated extensible type detector is useful. DetectReader fits a reader-based upload flow, and SetLimit controls detection reads. The library documents that the reader must begin at the start. Treat the result as classification, then perform decoder validation separately. The opened v1.4.16 documentation is dated October 17, 2026 and is later evidence.

6. **golang.org/x/image/draw** — https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/image/draw  
   Scale already decoded images with explicit interpolation choices to control the resizing speed/quality tradeoff. ApproxBiLinear and CatmullRom offer different compromises, documented by the package. This is a useful smaller building block if you want to assemble the decoding, allocation, resizing and encoding steps yourself. It supplies neither upload validation nor encoding. The inspected v0.48.0 documentation is dated November 9, 2026 and is later evidence.

7. **h2non/filetype** — https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/h2non/filetype  
   Infer image and MIME types from a short header prefix as a lightweight alternative to extension checks. Its documentation describes dependency-free recognition using a 262-byte prefix. This is an alternative to another MIME detector, not an additional mandatory layer. It does not validate a complete image stream. The inspected v1.1.3 documentation is dated November 21, 2021.

8. **imgproxy** — https://docs.imgproxy.net/configuration/options  
   Move image transformation into a dedicated service with configurable source-file, pixel, animation and result-size limits. This becomes relevant if you prefer serving transformed derivatives from a separate image-processing service. It adds service operation and source integration, so it is a larger architectural choice than a library in a Gin handler. Configure limits explicitly: the inspected documentation permits a zero source-file-size limit that disables that check. The opened 4.0.x documentation is live, with availability at the cutoff unverified.

## Suggested integration

My suggested composition is a bounded upload, an allowed-format decision, a header dimension check, a successful full decode, a resize, and encoding to a selected output format. Keep the decoded image from the validation step for transformation instead of doing the same full decode again. A header detector is optional if the decoder already supplies all the accepted-format information you need. Choose one resizing implementation initially, then measure representative files and concurrent uploads before adding native dependencies.

These are components and an integration proposal, not evidence of a tested deployment. The research used seven queries, including a blocked unauthenticated grep.app attempt, and twelve document-open attempts. Public code was subsequently found through web-indexed code search, and Go's source was opened directly. One excluded source-thread snippet appeared incidentally in the first search batch; it was recorded as an exposure and was not opened or used as supporting evidence.
